submissions.findingTextShort: Human single-dose data show alkamide absorption after Echinacea angustifolia root extract, not isolated-alkylamide efficacy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized open single-dose crossover pharmacokinetic study in 11 healthy adults measured six alkamides after oral administration of a 60% ethanolic Echinacea angustifolia root extract and detected the main dodecatetraenoic acid isobutylamides in plasma, with peak concentration occurring rapidly after dosing. This establishes systemic exposure to alkamides from a parent-botanical extract but does not test or establish clinical efficacy of isolated alkylamides.
submissions.populationContext: Eleven healthy adults in a randomized open single-dose crossover pharmacokinetic study.
submissions.usageContext: 60% ethanolic Echinacea angustifolia root extract; parent-botanical exposure rather than isolated alkylamide administration.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Pharmacokinetic exposure is not an efficacy endpoint, and the intervention contains the full extract matrix. Do not infer treatment benefit, isolated-constituent dosing, or broad safety. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: Echinacea-tablet pharmacokinetics show oral alkamide availability but do not establish an isolated-alkylamide consumer dose.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A human pharmacokinetic study measured alkamides after ingestion of tablets manufactured from ethanolic Echinacea angustifolia and Echinacea purpurea extracts. Alkamides were detectable in plasma within 20 minutes and remained detectable for hours, supporting oral availability from this mixed botanical preparation. The study did not administer isolated alkylamides as a consumer intervention and cannot establish an isolated-alkylamide efficacy or dosing recommendation.
submissions.populationContext: Nine healthy volunteers were studied after tablet ingestion with a standard high-fat breakfast, with two additional fasted subjects receiving the same preparation.
submissions.usageContext: Tablets made from ethanolic extracts of Echinacea angustifolia and Echinacea purpurea; exposure context only.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The pharmacokinetic result is preparation-specific and does not prove efficacy, optimal dose, long-term safety, or equivalence to purified alkylamides. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: A topical Echinacea purpurea alkylamide-containing extract cream improved selected atopic-eczema outcomes, with strict route and product limits.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: Randomized double-blind clinical studies evaluated a proprietary topical Echinacea purpurea-derived alkylamide-containing extract formulated in a water-in-oil cream for atopic eczema. The extract-based cream reduced local SCORAD versus comparator and was reported as well tolerated in the studied topical context. This is route- and formulation-specific evidence for an Echinacea-derived extract product and does not establish oral efficacy, isolated-alkylamide efficacy, or general safety of alkylamides as a compound class.
submissions.populationContext: Human topical clinical studies in participants with atopic eczema, plus a separate cutaneous tolerability assessment.
submissions.usageContext: Proprietary Echinacea purpurea-derived extract in a topical water-in-oil emulsion; not swallowed isolated alkylamides.
submissions.safetyContext: Reported topical tolerability applies only to the studied cream and exposure context and must not be generalized to oral or isolated alkylamide use.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The work was financially supported by Dr. August Wolff GmbH & Co. KG; several authors were sponsor employees and inventors on a related patent application. Product specificity, topical route, sponsorship, and extract composition materially limit generalization. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: A positive common-cold RCT used a multi-constituent Echinacea preparation, so its effect cannot be assigned to alkylamides alone.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled common-cold trial tested the standardized Echinilin Echinacea preparation containing alkamides, cichoric acid, and polysaccharides together and reported lower symptom scores in protocol-adherent participants. Because the intervention was a multi-constituent Echinacea product, the clinical result cannot be attributed specifically to alkylamides or used as evidence that isolated alkylamides are an effective cold treatment.
submissions.populationContext: Adults aged 18 to 65 with naturally acquired common colds; 282 were enrolled and 128 developed a cold during the trial.
submissions.usageContext: Standardized multi-constituent Echinacea preparation containing alkamides plus cichoric acid and polysaccharides; not an isolated-alkylamide intervention.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Component attribution is not possible from this design. The finding should remain a constituent-inheritance guard rather than a positive isolated-alkylamide claim. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: A large alkamide-standardized Echinacea trial found no statistically significant cold-severity or duration benefit versus placebo.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized controlled common-cold trial enrolled 719 participants and used Echinacea purpurea and Echinacea angustifolia root tablets standardized to alkamide content. In the blinded comparison, lower illness severity and shorter duration trends did not reach statistical significance. This parent-botanical null or mixed result must remain visible alongside positive Echinacea-product trials and cannot be translated into either efficacy or inefficacy of isolated alkylamides.
submissions.populationContext: Seven hundred nineteen participants aged 12 to 80 with new-onset common cold were randomized; 713 completed the protocol.
submissions.usageContext: Echinacea purpurea and Echinacea angustifolia root tablets standardized to alkamide content; multi-constituent botanical intervention.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The study was designed to test the Echinacea formulation rather than isolated alkylamides, and higher-than-expected variability limited power to detect small benefits. Preserve the null/mixed product-level result without assigning causality to a constituent. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.

submissions.findingTextShort: Echinacea alkylamides show CB2-predominant receptor and cytokine effects in mechanistic systems, not clinical efficacy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: Mechanistic experiments found that selected Echinacea alkylamides bind cannabinoid receptors with stronger affinity for CB2 than CB1 and modulate cytokine responses in cellular and ex vivo human-blood systems. These receptor and cytokine findings support a mechanistic hypothesis only; they do not establish clinical efficacy, an effective human dose, or consumer safety for isolated alkylamides.
submissions.mechanismContext: Selected isolated Echinacea alkylamides were evaluated in receptor-binding, cellular signaling, and cytokine-expression experiments; CB2-independent effects were also observed.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: In-vitro and ex-vivo pharmacology cannot be upgraded into human clinical efficacy. The mixed CB2-dependent and independent findings also argue against a simplistic single-receptor mechanism claim. The source remains draft-only until canonical source registration and semantic attestation are complete.
